slides.title: What does one row represent?
slides.context: Three separate synthetic files contain purchases, deliveries and branches. Their rows have different meanings.
slides.line: Can the first row of each file be treated as one customer?
points: Name the unit recorded in each file before joining or averaging.
A matching row number does not establish a real-world relationship.

slides.title: Choose the unit before the summary
slides.context: Purchase file A has 12 order values; delivery file B has 5 durations per supplier; branch file C has paired advertising and sales.
slides.line: One order · one delivery · one branch
points: Twelve orders need not mean twelve distinct customers.
Keep each branch's advertising and sales values paired in the same row.

slides.title: Check values before calculating
slides.context: The three files use dollars, days and thousands of dollars, respectively.
slides.line: A zero is observed; a blank may be unknown
points: Check units, missing values, duplicates and comparable time periods.
Supplier names are categories: count them or compare the days within them.

slides.title: Which total belongs below the fraction?
slides.context: A separate shop records 100 orders: 50 online, 30 in store and 20 by phone.
slides.line: What share of all orders came by phone?
points: Use the count of phone orders in the numerator.
Name the entire group of orders before choosing the denominator.

slides.title: Online accounts for half the orders
slides.context: Synthetic channel counts for 100 separate shop orders; each bar measures orders, not dollars.

slides.title: A frequency table keeps counts and shares together
slides.context: The synthetic 100-order channel table has 50 online, 30 in-store and 20 phone orders.
points: Counts sum to 100 and shares sum to 1.
Each order must belong to exactly one of these channel categories.

slides.title: The word ‘of’ selects the denominator
slides.context: In a separate 80-order payment table, 30 orders are both online and card-paid; 40 are online.
points: Among all 80 orders, the same 30 count as 30/80 = 37.5%.
The numerator must belong to the group named by the denominator.

slides.title: What can the channel bars actually show?
slides.context: The chart uses counts from the separate 100-order shop: online 50, in store 30, phone 20.
slides.line: Does the tallest bar identify the highest revenue?
points: Each bar measures orders, not dollars.
Predict the largest order count before making a revenue claim.

slides.title: A bar's length represents its count
slides.context: The channel chart shows 50 online, 30 in-store and 20 phone orders on a shared scale starting at zero.
slides.line: 50/20 = 2.5: online has 2.5 times as many orders as phone
points: A zero baseline keeps bar-length comparisons honest.
The table supplies exact counts; the chart makes the pattern easier to see.

slides.title: A count chart cannot answer a revenue question
slides.context: The shop's channel summary reports order counts only; individual order values are absent.
points: Revenue needs order values or totals for each channel.
The chart also cannot establish what next month's customers will do.

slides.title: Does revenue per order describe a typical basket?
slides.context: Twelve original purchase values total $540; eleven are $18–$46 and one is $200.
slides.line: If every order shared revenue equally, what would each receive?
points: Divide the total by the number of orders.
Then ask whether that equal share resembles most observed orders.

slides.title: The mean shares the total across all orders
slides.context: The twelve purchases sum to $540, including the $200 purchase.
points: The mean uses every value and reconstructs the total: 12 × $45 = $540.
$45 is an equal-share calculation, not a newly observed purchase.

slides.title: A large order pulls the mean upward
slides.context: Eleven of twelve purchase values are at most $46, while the final purchase is $200.
points: Keep the mean for revenue planning because it retains the total.
Use a positional summary to describe a more ordinary basket.

slides.title: Where is the middle of twelve purchases?
slides.context: The sorted purchases have $30 at position 6 and $32 at position 7.
slides.line: For an even count, which two positions bracket the middle?
points: Sort the values before finding a position.
There are six purchases on each side of the central gap.

slides.title: Average the two central values for an even count
slides.context: In the sorted twelve-purchase file, positions 6 and 7 contain $30 and $32.
points: No purchase needs to equal the median.
The median identifies position; it does not reconstruct total revenue.

slides.title: Moving an extreme value need not move the median
slides.context: The largest purchase is $200; hypothetically replace it with $50 while all other values stay fixed.
points: The median stays $31 because the central positions do not move.
The mean changes because the total revenue changes.

slides.title: Which amount occurs most often?
slides.context: Every one of the original twelve purchase amounts appears exactly once.
slides.line: Does this file have a repeated mode?
points: Count repetitions of each value.
A largest value is not necessarily a most frequent value.

slides.title: The mode is the most frequent value or category
slides.context: A separate five-purchase book contains $10, $10, $20, $20 and $30.
points: Both $10 and $20 are modes in this practice book.
Under this course's convention, the original all-unique file has no repeated mode.

slides.title: Choose the summary that answers the question
slides.context: The original purchase file has mean $45, median $31 and no repeated mode.
slides.line: Total planning → mean; central basket → median
points: Use the mode to name a commonly repeated value or category when one exists.
Do not average category names or confuse the largest value with the mode.

slides.title: Does one extreme purchase define the spread?
slides.context: The purchase file runs from $18 to $200; most values lie much closer together.
slides.line: How can we describe the middle half separately?
points: The range uses only the two extremes.
Quartiles mark positions within the ordered values.

slides.title: The IQR measures the middle half
slides.context: Using the course's exclusive-quartile convention, Q1 = $24.25 and Q3 = $41.
points: State the quartile convention because software can interpolate differently.
The range is $200 − $18 = $182, a different spread summary.

slides.title: An outlier fence is a flag for investigation
slides.context: For these purchases, Q3 = $41 and IQR = $16.75; one order is $200.
points: $200 lies above the fence and should be checked.
A flag alone does not justify deleting a valid purchase.

slides.title: Can equal means hide different delivery risk?
slides.context: Suppliers A and B each average five days; A has 4,5,5,5,6 and B has 1,2,5,8,9 days.
slides.line: Which supplier misses a six-day target more often here?
points: ‘Within six days’ includes day 6.
Count observed misses before comparing spread formulas.

slides.title: Equal means conceal different late counts
slides.context: These five deliveries per supplier are separate synthetic observations. A target miss occurs after day six.

slides.title: Square gaps so opposite deviations do not cancel
slides.context: Both suppliers mean five days. A's squared deviations sum to 2 days²; B's sum to 50 days².
points: Divide by five to describe these five recorded deliveries per supplier.
Estimating a wider population's variance from a sample usually uses n − 1.

slides.title: Spread and target misses answer different questions
slides.context: A has no deliveries later than six days; B has two of five later than six days.
points: B's descriptive variance is larger, but variance is measured in days squared.
Five records per supplier do not guarantee the same rates in future deliveries.

slides.title: How can spread return to days?
slides.context: Descriptive variances are 0.4 days² for A and 10 days² for B.
slides.line: What operation reverses the squared unit?
points: Variance records squared deviations.
A delivery decision is easier to read in days.

slides.title: Standard deviation uses the original units
slides.context: Using the five observed deliveries for each supplier, A's variance is 0.4 and B's is 10 days².
points: B's SD is five times A's, not 25 times.
SD is a spread summary, not a maximum delay or promised delivery window.

slides.title: CV compares spread relative to a meaningful mean
slides.context: Both supplier means are five days; their descriptive SDs are about 0.63 and 3.16 days.
points: Use CV for positive ratio-scale measurements with a meaningful zero.
Near-zero means make CV unstable; it is not a substitute for the day-scale SD.

slides.title: Which side contains the distant order?
slides.context: A separate practice shop has five purchases: $10, $10, $10, $10 and $30.
slides.line: Would its asymmetry point left or right?
points: The mean is $14; four orders sit just below it.
The single $30 order lies farther above the mean.

slides.title: Signed cubes preserve the direction of imbalance
slides.context: The practice values have mean $14 and descriptive SD $8; standardized gaps are four −0.5s and one +2.
points: The distant right-side purchase contributes a large positive cube.
Reflecting the data swaps the sign while keeping the SD the same.

slides.title: Skewness describes shape, not business quality
slides.context: The five-purchase practice example has positive moment skewness of 1.5.
slides.line: Positive skew → a longer or heavier right side here
points: A sign and one number do not replace a plot of the values.
Check units, sample size and outliers before interpreting the shape.

slides.title: What does a fourth power emphasize?
slides.context: Reuse the practice purchases: four $10 orders and one $30 order, with mean $14 and SD $8.
slides.line: Which contributes more: a gap of 0.5 SD or 2 SD?
points: Standardize each gap before raising it to the fourth power.
Fourth powers are nonnegative and magnify distant values.

slides.title: The distant value dominates the fourth moment
slides.context: Four purchases are 0.5 SD from the mean; one is 2 SD from it.
points: The single distant order contributes 16 of the 16.25 total.
This is population-moment kurtosis for the five-value teaching example.

slides.title: Kurtosis needs a definition and a plot
slides.context: The five-value teaching example has raw kurtosis 3.25 under the displayed moment convention.
points: Raw and excess kurtosis differ by three; say which one is reported.
A small sample's fourth moment is sensitive to a distant value.

slides.title: Do the paired branch values move together?
slides.context: Five branches pair advertising and sales in $ thousands; the sample means are 3 and 6, respectively.
slides.line: Does a branch above both means add a positive or negative product?
points: Subtract each variable's own mean.
Multiply deviations from the same branch; do not break the pairs.

slides.title: Covariance averages paired deviation products
slides.context: For the five original branch pairs, the centered cross-products sum to 7 in squared thousands of dollars.
points: Same-sign gaps add positive products; opposite-sign gaps add negative ones.
Covariance's units combine both variables' units and depend on their scales.

slides.title: A positive covariance is an association
slides.context: The five paired branches show a positive descriptive covariance of 1.4 in the chosen units.
slides.line: Together in these records ≠ caused by advertising
points: A larger branch could spend more and sell more for another reason.
Standardize the paired association before comparing its strength across scales.

slides.title: Would the association survive a unit change?
slides.context: The five branch pairs have centered cross-product total 7; advertising and sales squared-gap totals are 10 and 18.
slides.line: What happens if advertising is recorded in dollars instead of $ thousands?
points: Covariance changes when one variable's units change.
Correlation removes both measurement scales.

slides.title: Correlation standardizes the paired co-movement
slides.context: For the five branches, centered cross-products sum to 7; squared deviations total 10 and 18.
points: This is a positive but imperfect linear association in the sample.
Its value stays between −1 and 1 and has no measurement unit.

slides.title: Correlation does not estimate an ad return
slides.context: Advertising and sales were measured in the same period for five branches; r ≈ 0.52.
slides.line: Observed association ≠ incremental sales caused by ads
points: Branch size, location or demand may explain part of the pattern.
A causal claim needs a defensible design or experiment, not r alone.

slides.title: What would you tell the manager?
slides.context: Purchases have mean $45 and median $31; supplier A has fewer observed late deliveries; branch r is about 0.52.
slides.line: Which result supports an action, and what remains uncertain?
points: Use one piece of evidence for each recommendation.
State a next check and a limit before promising an outcome.

slides.title: A useful briefing has three parts
slides.context: The course's purchase, delivery and branch files are separate synthetic datasets.
points: For purchases, use median $31 for an ordinary basket and mean $45 for revenue planning; verify the $200 order.
For suppliers, compare spread and target misses only after checking product, route and service terms.

slides.title: End with a claim the data can support
slides.context: The five branches have a positive sample correlation, but no measured causal advertising effect.
slides.line: Describe now; test before committing more spend
points: Report the observed association without calling it a return on advertising.
Propose a controlled test or stronger design and name the outcome to monitor.

slides.title: What number describes one pickup slot?
slides.context: A synthetic shop records the number of orders arriving in a slot; possible counts are 0, 1, 2 and 3.
slides.line: What is the random variable X?
points: Define the rule that maps a full outcome to a number.
A list of possible counts alone does not assign their chances.

slides.title: One number can collect several outcomes
slides.context: In a separate two-call example, N means no purchase and Y means a purchase on each call.
slides.line: NN → 0; NY or YN → 1; YY → 2 purchases
points: The support of this count is {0, 1, 2}.
Two different complete outcomes map to X = 1.

slides.title: Support and probability are separate
slides.context: The shop's pickup count allows 0–3 orders. The two-call example allows 0–2 purchases.
points: Keep the two teaching examples separate.
A probability model or data are needed before estimating a chance.

slides.title: Which bars belong to the event?
slides.line: Is ‘at least two’ one bar or two?
points: Write the included counts before adding probabilities.
The four masses must total one.

slides.title: The PMF shows each count's chance
slides.context: The original synthetic pickup-slot model assigns probabilities to 0, 1, 2 and 3 orders.

slides.title: A PMF assigns mass to each possible count
slides.context: For shop orders per slot, p(0)=0.10, p(1)=0.30, p(2)=0.40 and p(3)=0.20.
points: Exactly two orders has chance p(2) = 0.40.
At most two includes 0, 1 and 2, giving 0.80.

slides.title: Check a PMF before using it
slides.context: The four shop masses are 0.10, 0.30, 0.40 and 0.20.
points: A negative entry or a total other than one is not a valid PMF.
The probabilities are specified teaching assumptions, not measured shop rates.

slides.title: What does capacity two cover?
slides.context: In the shop model, the masses for 0, 1, 2 and 3 orders are 0.10, 0.30, 0.40 and 0.20.
slides.line: Which counts are at or below two?
points: Include the capacity boundary itself.
Add the corresponding masses to obtain coverage.

slides.title: Cumulative chance grows with capacity
slides.context: The shop's CDF adds every count at or below each capacity. Its discrete jumps are intentional.

slides.title: The CDF adds probabilities up to a cutoff
slides.context: The shop model has P(X=0)=0.10, P(X=1)=0.30 and P(X=2)=0.40.
points: Capacity two covers 80% of slots under this model.
Demand above two has chance 1 − F(2) = 0.20.

slides.title: For integer counts, endpoints matter
slides.context: The shop CDF has F(1)=0.40, F(2)=0.80 and F(3)=1.
points: Subtract F(1), not F(2), because ‘at least two’ includes two.
To cover at least 81% of slots, capacity must rise to three.

slides.title: Can expected demand be a fractional order?
slides.context: The shop model permits 0, 1, 2 or 3 orders with masses 0.10, 0.30, 0.40 and 0.20.
slides.line: Must the mean be one of the possible counts?
points: Weight each possible count by its chance.
Interpret the result over many comparable slots, not as one slot's outcome.

slides.title: Expectation is a probability-weighted average
slides.context: The shop's specified masses for 0–3 orders are 0.10, 0.30, 0.40 and 0.20.
points: The units are orders per slot.
The average 1.7 need not occur in any single slot.

slides.title: Expected totals do not promise observed totals
slides.context: If 100 slots share the shop's 1.7-order mean, linearity gives their expected total.
points: Expectation adds even when slots are dependent.
The actual total can differ; variability still matters to staffing.

slides.title: How much can demand vary around 1.7?
slides.context: The shop's possible order counts are 0–3, with specified probabilities 0.10, 0.30, 0.40 and 0.20.
points: Signed gaps above and below the mean would cancel.
Weight each squared gap by its probability.

slides.title: Model variance weights squared gaps
slides.context: The shop model has E[X] = 1.7 orders and specified masses for 0–3 orders.
points: Its SD is √0.81 = 0.90 orders.
No sample n − 1 correction belongs to a fully specified PMF.

slides.title: Scaling changes spread; shifting does not
slides.context: For a payoff Y = a + bX, a is fixed and b multiplies the order count X.
points: Adding a fixed amount moves the mean without changing variance.
Doubling every gap doubles SD and multiplies variance by four.

slides.title: Can two 50% busy rates hide a shared rush?
slides.context: In a separate counter model, A and B each have a 50% chance of being busy.
slides.line: Do those two marginals fix P(both busy)?
points: A marginal describes one counter at a time.
The joint cells tell us how the two states occur together.

slides.title: Read a joint cell, then its row total
slides.context: An illustrative independent table has four joint cells of 0.25 for the two binary busy indicators.
points: The cell is joint; adding across the row gives a marginal.
Conditioning on A = 1 gives P(B=1 | A=1)=.25/.50=.50.

slides.title: Matching marginals do not imply independence
slides.context: Another joint table has cells 0.45, 0.05, 0.05 and 0.45, while both busy marginals remain 0.50.
points: A common rush could make simultaneous staffing needs more likely.

slides.title: Does dependence change total workload risk?
slides.context: Two counters each have busy probability 0.5; their joint both-busy chance q may vary.
slides.line: Can the expected busy count stay one while its spread changes?
points: Separate each counter's marginal risk from their co-movement.
Compare an alternating pattern with a shared rush.

slides.title: Covariance links the joint chance to the total
slides.context: A and B are binary busy indicators with P(A=1)=P(B=1)=0.5; q=P(A=1,B=1).
points: If q=.45, covariance is .20 and total variance is .90.
If q=.05, covariance is −.20 and total variance is .10.

slides.title: Zero covariance need not mean independence
slides.context: A separate teaching example has X equally likely at −1, 0 and 1, with Y=X².
slides.line: Cov(X,Y)=0, yet Y is determined by X
points: Positive and negative deviation products cancel here.
Independence requires the entire joint distribution to factor.

slides.title: Which process produced the count?
slides.context: Separate examples count purchases among visits, tagged items in a finite draw, and orders arriving over time.
slides.line: Fixed trials, draws without replacement, or a time window?
points: Choose the mechanism before its named distribution.
Keep these examples separate from the shop's four-bar PMF.

slides.title: Binomial counts successes in fixed independent trials
slides.context: In a separate example, 12 visitors independently buy with the same probability p=0.25.
points: The model needs a fixed trial count and one success/failure outcome per visit.
If p varies or visits depend on each other, reconsider the model.

slides.title: Without replacement, the composition changes
slides.context: A finite lot has 40 distinct items, 8 tagged; select 6 without replacement.
points: Choose one tagged item and five untagged items, then divide by all six-item draws.
Success chances change across draws, so an ordinary binomial model is unsuitable.

slides.title: What is the exposure window?
slides.context: A separate homogeneous arrival model has an average rate of four orders per hour.
slides.line: What mean count belongs to half an hour?
points: Multiply the rate by the window length in matching units.
A time-window count is different from fractional hours of downtime.

slides.title: Poisson counts arrivals in a fixed window
slides.context: At four orders per hour, a half-hour window has mean λ=4×0.5=2 orders.
points: Poisson support is 0,1,2,…; under the model, mean and variance both equal λ.
The rate and independent-increment assumptions must fit the process.

slides.title: Add counts before taking a tail
slides.context: The half-hour Poisson model has λ=2 orders.
points: At most two includes counts 0, 1 and 2.
Clustering, batches or a changing rate can break the simple model.

slides.title: Can a density be taller than one?
slides.context: A separate pickup wait is uniform from 0 to 0.5 hours.
slides.line: Its density is 2 per hour: is that valid?
points: Probability is area, not density height.
Check width times height across the full interval.

slides.title: Continuous probability comes from area
slides.context: For T uniform on [0,0.5] hours, f(t)=2 per hour within the interval.
points: The full area's 2×0.5=1, so the density is valid.
A single exact time has zero interval width and zero probability.

slides.title: A continuous CDF accumulates area
slides.context: The same uniform wait has density 2 per hour between zero and half an hour.
points: The CDF is zero below the window and one above it.
F(0.25)=0.50 matches the first quarter-hour area.

slides.title: Is waiting bounded or open-ended?
slides.context: Separate examples model pickup between 2 and 8 minutes and the wait for an arrival at rate 0.1 per minute.
slides.line: Which assumption rules out a 9-minute wait?
points: A uniform 2–8 minute window has a hard upper bound.
An exponential wait can be longer than any fixed cutoff.

slides.title: A uniform window makes interval length decisive
slides.context: T is uniform from 2 to 8 minutes, so its density is 1/6 per minute.
points: Its mean is 5 minutes and variance is 3 minutes².
These conclusions require equal density across the bounded interval.

slides.title: An exponential wait has a constant hazard
slides.context: In a separate Poisson process, the arrival rate is 0.1 per minute and the mean wait is 10 minutes.
points: Memorylessness says another 10-minute wait has the same survival chance after already waiting.
That property is a model assumption, not a general rule for real queues.

slides.title: Where is 496 mL on the normal scale?
slides.context: A separate filling model assumes X is normal with mean 500 mL and SD 4 mL.
slides.line: How many SDs below the mean is 496 mL?
points: Subtract the mean before dividing by SD.
State the event as a left-tail or interval question.

slides.title: Standardization puts a cutoff on a common scale
slides.context: The filling model assumes mean 500 mL and SD 4 mL.
points: Φ is the standard-normal cumulative distribution function.
The result depends on the assumed normal shape, including its tails.

slides.title: Subtract CDF values for an interval
slides.context: The filling model has mean 500 mL and SD 4 mL; 496 and 504 are one SD from the mean.
points: Write both endpoints before using the normal CDF.
This probability describes the model, not a guarantee for every production run.

slides.title: Which cutoff leaves only 5% above it?
slides.context: For the normal filling model, mean is 500 mL and SD is 4 mL.
slides.line: A 5% upper tail starts at which cumulative percentage?
points: Translate the right-tail request into a left-tail CDF level.
Then return from standard-normal units to mL.

slides.title: Invert the CDF, then undo standardization
slides.context: A 5% right tail means cumulative probability 0.95 in the normal model.
points: Φ⁻¹(.95)≈1.6449 is a standard-normal cutoff.
A one-sided 95th percentile is not a central 95% interval endpoint.

slides.title: A central 95% interval splits both tails
slides.context: The normal filling model has mean 500 mL and SD 4 mL.
points: The upper endpoint uses 97.5% cumulative probability, not 95%.
Check whether the normal model is appropriate before using tail cutoffs operationally.

slides.title: Can a mean below capacity rule out overload?
slides.context: Return to the shop PMF: demand is 0–3 orders with masses .10, .30, .40 and .20; capacity is 2.
slides.line: Mean demand is 1.7: can overload still occur?
points: Compare each possible demand with capacity, not only the mean.
Overload occurs when X is greater than two.

slides.title: Tail risk remains when the mean fits
slides.context: The shop has P(X=3)=0.20 and one worker can handle two orders per slot.
points: Only the three-order outcome exceeds capacity, by one order.
Apply a nonlinear excess rule to each outcome before averaging.

slides.title: Compare expected consequences, not just workload
slides.context: Hypothetical costs: $30 per excess order versus $8 per slot for an extra worker; expected excess is .20.
points: Under these teaching costs, the extra worker has higher expected cost.
At $50 per excess order, expected delay cost becomes $10 and the decision reverses.

slides.title: Why are sample summaries random?
slides.context: Different samples from the same population can produce different means and variances.
slides.line: What distribution describes a statistic across samples?
points: A statistic is a function of the selected observations.
Its variation is new uncertainty beyond one modeled outcome.

slides.title: Chi-square and t describe different uncertainty
slides.context: Let independent Z values be standard normal; let U be their squared sum with ν terms.
points: For t, Z must be independent of U; the estimated scale creates heavier tails.
Degrees of freedom count the independent squared terms in this construction.

slides.title: F compares two independently estimated scales
slides.context: Let U and V be independent chi-square quantities with m and n degrees of freedom.
points: The ratio is positive and the numerator–denominator order matters.
Later classes use sampling distributions to quantify uncertainty in estimates and tests.
